title: How to Find a Psychologist in Sydney Who Understands Your Background
description: Find a Sydney psychologist who offers sessions in your preferred language, and ask how they would approach a family commitment before you book.
author: Sonia Kaurah
article_html:
Quick answers

How can you choose a psychologist who understands your background?

Start with what brings you to therapy and what you want your psychologist to understand. If you want to speak Cantonese in sessions, search by language and suburb, then confirm with the individual psychologist.

How can you tell whether a psychologist understands your values?

Notice how the psychologist responds when you explain a family commitment. If you help pay your parents’ rent, do they ask what you want help with, or assume you want to stop?

In this article

  1. What Do You Want Your Psychologist to Understand?
  2. Where Can You Look for a Psychologist in Sydney?
  3. What Can You Ask Before You Book?
  4. Did You Feel Understood in the First Session?
  5. References

What Do You Want Your Psychologist to Understand?

You might switch languages halfway through a sentence about home because the word you need is not in English. Before searching in Sydney, we suggest deciding whether you want sessions in that language or a psychologist who understands why you might switch.

It is reasonable to prefer someone from your community. A shared background alone cannot tell you how they will respond. Try writing down what brings you to therapy and what you’d like your psychologist to understand about your background.

This guidance is for planned appointments. For immediate crisis support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. If life is in danger, call 000.

Where Can You Look for a Psychologist in Sydney?

Start with a suburb you can get to around work. If you want to speak Cantonese in therapy, for example, try searching for “Cantonese speaking psychologist Chatswood”. If you find few options, try nearby suburbs or consider telehealth before dropping the language requirement.

You can also tell your GP what brings you to therapy and what you want a psychologist to understand about your background. Ask whom they would suggest. Healthdirect lists Medicare Mental Health as a service that gives advice and can connect you with local mental health services. You will still need to ask about cultural fit.

What Can You Learn From a Profile?

Read the individual psychologist’s profile for the languages they use in sessions and their experience with the concern that brought you to therapy. If a group practice lists your preferred language, ask whether the psychologist you would see offers sessions in it.

Do not infer someone’s background from a photo or surname. Separately, look for the psychologist’s registration number in their profile or ask the practice for it. If their experience looks relevant but the profile leaves your cultural priority unanswered, ask about it before you book.

What Can You Ask Before You Book?

We suggest asking how the psychologist would approach a specific concern. You can ask by email or phone. Share only enough to make the question clear. You do not need to explain your family history or speak for your community.

Before booking, ask the practice what it charges per session and what you would pay after any rebate you qualify for. Check whether there is an appointment time that fits around work. If you and the psychologist belong to the same community and you are concerned about privacy, ask how they would handle running into you outside the practice.

Hypothetical example
Talking about the pressure of helping with rent
You could ask: “I help pay my parents’ rent. How would we talk about the financial pressure without assuming I want to stop helping?”
A useful reply would explain how the psychologist would ask what paying the rent means to you and what you want help with. A general assurance that they welcome people from all cultures leaves you without a sense of how they would handle that conversation.
Give more weight to a reply that shows how the psychologist would work with the goal you set.

Did You Feel Understood in the First Session?

Recall an exchange about your background. Notice whether the psychologist asked what was important to you, left room for you to disagree and used your answer to decide with you what to work on. If they did, consider booking again.

A respectful question can help. If you raise a misunderstanding, notice whether they listen and adjust. If you keep having to defend a value or correct a stereotype, you can contact someone else without explaining why.

About the author

Sonia Kaurah

Founder & CEO - Tala Thrive | Ex VC | Board Member | Building Culturally Competent Mental Health Care | Rising Star 2024 Award Winner | Public Speaker

References

  1. Mental health helplines | healthdirect
  2. Lifeline crisis support - 13 11 14

This article is general information and should be adapted to your circumstances.
